Winston Churchill. The paramount wartime leader of the twentieth century, rallying Britain to resist Nazi Germany when defeat seemed imminent.

Churchill became Prime Minister in May 1940 when Nazi Germany was advancing across Europe and France was collapsing. His refusal to negotiate with Hitler and his rhetoric of defiance stiffened British resolve in the nation's darkest hour. His oratory, combative resolve, and romantic vision of British power became synonymous with defiance and leadership during the Second World War.

He forged the Special Relationship with the United States, convincing President Roosevelt to support Britain before America entered the war and securing the Atlantic alliance that defeated Nazi Germany. This partnership proved crucial to ultimate victory.

After the war, Churchill remained a commanding voice on the world stage. He coined the term Iron Curtain in a 1946 speech to describe Soviet domination of Eastern Europe, helping to define Cold War rhetoric and justify Western rearmament. He served as Prime Minister again from 1951 to 1955, presiding over Britain's adjustment to its diminished postwar status and the loss of empire, particularly the independence of India.

Churchill won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1953 for his massive multi-volume history of the Second World War, a work of strategic analysis wrapped in grand narrative. He remains the most recognizable British statesman of the modern era, iconic as both a warrior and a man of letters, forever defined by his leadership during humanity's darkest hours.
